The user wants to rename a git branch both locally and on the remote, and they mentioned they lose track of long instructions — so the ADHD output style applies: numbered steps, short, lead with the action, one concrete next action at the end. This is also a "give me the steps" request, so a numbered list of commands is exactly right.

The situation: branch is `feature-x`, should be `auth-refactor`, already pushed to origin. They're presumably currently on `feature-x` (likely, since they named it and are working on it). I should account for the case where they're on it — `git branch -m` works when on the branch. If not on it, the syntax is `git branch -m old new`. I'll give the simplest path assuming they're on it, since that's the most common case, and keep it tight.

Steps:
1. Rename locally: `git branch -m auth-refactor` (works if on feature-x; if on another branch, `git branch -m feature-x auth-refactor`)
2. Push the new name: `git push origin -u auth-refactor`
3. Delete the old remote branch: `git push origin --delete feature-x`

Caveats worth one line: if a PR exists for feature-x, renaming closes nothing but the PR still points at the old branch — actually on GitHub, if you delete the old remote branch, an open PR targeting/from it gets closed automatically. So worth one warning: open PR from feature-x will close when the old branch is deleted; GitHub also now supports renaming a branch from the web UI which updates PRs. But per rule 4 (suppress tangents), keep it to one short warning line. Also teammates who checked out feature-x — probably out of scope for a solo dev; skip or fold into one line.

Also note: the working directory isn't a git repo per the environment, so I can't verify anything — this is a pure advice answer, which is fine.

content.text:
1. Rename it locally (run this while on `feature-x`):
   ```
   git branch -m auth-refactor
   ```
   If you're on a different branch, use `git branch -m feature-x auth-refactor` instead.

2. Push the new name and set it to track:
   ```
   git push origin -u auth-refactor
   ```

3. Delete the old branch on the remote:
   ```
   git push origin --delete feature-x
   ```

One warning: if there's an open pull request from `feature-x`, deleting the remote branch will close it. In that case rename the branch on GitHub instead (Branches page → pencil icon next to `feature-x`) — that updates the PR automatically — then run `git branch -m auth-refactor` locally and `git fetch --prune`.

Takes about a minute. Next: run step 1 and paste any error you get.
